The shop also maintains I-CAR Gold Class and I-CAR Platinum recognition. | What Is Frame Damage? | Frame damage occurs when collision forces affect structural components that contribute to the vehicle’s: | Load carrying | Crash-energy management | Occupant compartment | Suspension mounting | Safety-system mounting | On a traditional body-on-frame vehicle, those components can include: | Frame rails | Crossmembers | Brackets | Mounting points | On a unibody vehicle, structural areas may include: | Front rails | Rear rails | Rocker panels | Pillars | Floor sections | Roof rails | Reinforcements | Suspension mounting areas | For example, Ford currently defines structural repair as repair or replacement involving parts that carry crash energy or vehicle loads, form part of the occupant safety cell, provide safety-system attachment, or are factory welded, bonded, or riveted into the structure. | Is Frame Damage the Same on Every Vehicle? | No. | Vehicle construction varies significantly. | A pickup truck may use a separate ladder-style frame. | A sedan or crossover may use a unibody structure. | An electric vehicle may combine: | Aluminum | Advanced high-strength steels | Structural adhesives | Large battery-protection structures | That is why the technician first needs to identify the exact: | Year | Make | Model | Construction type | before determining how the damage should be repaired. | What Is Body-on-Frame Construction? | Body-on-frame construction uses a separate structural frame beneath the body. | The body and other major systems attach to that frame. | This design is common on many: | Pickup trucks | Large SUVs | Commercial vehicles | A collision can affect: | Frame rails | Crossmembers | Suspension attachment areas | Body mounts | Damage may require measurement and manufacturer-specific structural procedures. | What Is Unibody Construction? | A unibody vehicle integrates much of its body and structural support into one engineered assembly. | Rather than relying on one separate frame underneath, structural strength is distributed through areas such as: | Rails | Pillars | Rockers | Floors | Roof structures | Reinforcements | Many passenger vehicles use this design. | That means drivers may still hear the term “frame damage” even though the vehicle technically has a unibody structure. | What Causes Frame Damage? | Structural damage can result from: | Front-end collisions | Rear-end collisions | Side impacts | Rollover accidents | Multi-vehicle collisions | Impacts with fixed objects | Wheel or suspension impacts | The severity depends on more than speed. | Important factors include: | Impact direction | Impact height | Point of contact | Vehicle construction | Materials | Secondary impacts | Two vehicles with similar-looking exterior damage can have very different structural conditions underneath. | Can a Minor Collision Cause Frame Damage? | Potentially. | A low-speed bumper impact may affect only: | Bumper cover | Energy absorber | Reinforcement | Brackets | Another impact at similar speed may occur directly at a wheel, suspension mounting point, or structural corner. | The outward appearance does not always reveal the full damage pattern. | That does not mean every minor accident causes structural damage. | It means technicians should evaluate the actual impact rather than assuming damage severity from appearance alone. | What Are Common Signs of Frame or Structural Damage? | Possible signs can include: | Uneven panel gaps | Hood or trunk misalignment | Doors that rub or do not close normally | Vehicle pulling | Steering wheel off center | Uneven tire wear | Wheel position appearing different | New noises | Visible buckling or distortion | These signs do not automatically prove structural damage. | For example, pulling may also result from: | Tire damage | Wheel damage | Suspension damage | Alignment | Professional diagnosis is needed to determine the actual cause. | Why Do Panel Gaps Matter? | Panel relationships can provide clues about how the vehicle is positioned. | After a collision, look at gaps around: | Hood | Fender | Doors | Quarter panels | Trunk | Liftgate | If one side suddenly becomes much wider or tighter, technicians may investigate further. | However, panel gaps are not structural measurements. | A poor gap could come from: | Panel adjustment | Hinges | Brackets | Mounting points | Structural movement | That is why measurement can be necessary. | Can Doors Show Signs of Structural Damage? | Sometimes. | A door that suddenly: | Requires extra force to close | Rubs against another panel | Will not latch | Sits unevenly | may indicate damage involving: | Door | Hinge | Latch | Striker | Pillar | Rocker | Structure | The symptom should be investigated rather than used as proof of one specific problem. | Can Frame Damage Affect Wheel Alignment? | Yes. | Suspension systems rely on accurate mounting locations. | If collision damage moves: | Suspension mounting points | Structural rails | Crossmembers | Wheel alignment can change. | Possible symptoms can include: | Vehicle pulling | Steering wheel off center | Uneven tire wear | Handling changes | The alignment problem should be traced to its cause rather than simply adjusted without evaluating damaged components. | How Do Collision Repair Technicians Identify Frame Damage? | The process can include: | Visual inspection | Disassembly | Damage analysis | Computerized measuring | OEM repair research | Suspension evaluation | Structural measurement becomes especially important when technicians need to determine whether reference points remain within manufacturer specifications. | I-CAR’s current | OEM Technical Information Matrix | organizes manufacturer-specific information around topics such as body construction materials, repair guidelines, sectioning procedures, attachment methods, and corrosion protection. | What Is 3D Structural Measuring? | Three-dimensional measuring compares structural reference points with vehicle specifications. | Instead of relying only on appearance, technicians can evaluate whether important areas have moved. | Measurements can help determine: | Where movement occurred | How significant it is | Whether correction is needed | Whether the repair is progressing correctly | Whether final dimensions are within applicable specifications | Certain OEM guidance specifically calls for structural distortion to be corrected using proper straightening equipment and a three-dimensional measuring system. | Can You See Frame Damage Just by Looking at the Car? | Not always. | Severe deformation can be obvious. | Smaller dimensional changes may not be. | A vehicle may appear straight while one or more structural reference points remain outside specification. | The opposite can also happen. | A bolt-on panel may look crooked even when the underlying structure is correct. | That is why structural measurements provide information that visual inspection alone cannot. | What Happens After Structural Damage Is Identified? | Technicians need to determine the appropriate repair method. | Depending on the vehicle and component, the repair can involve: | Straightening | Replacement | Sectioning where permitted | Welding | Riveting | Structural adhesive | A combination of these methods | There is no single structural repair technique that applies to every vehicle. | Can a Bent Frame Be Straightened? | Sometimes. | Certain components may be straightened when: | The manufacturer permits it | The material allows it | Damage falls within repairable limits | Specialized structural equipment can be used to apply controlled force. | Measurements may be taken throughout the process. | The goal is not simply to pull the vehicle until it looks straight. | The repair should be guided by: | OEM procedures | Material limitations | Dimensional data | What Is a Frame Rack? | A frame rack or structural repair system allows technicians to: | Secure the vehicle | Apply controlled pulling forces | Access damaged areas | Measure structural points | Although people often call this equipment a “frame machine,” it can also be used on unibody vehicles. | The machine is only one part of the repair. | Accurate measurements and manufacturer-specific procedures remain essential. | Can Every Bent Frame Rail Be Straightened? | No. | Repairability depends on: | Material | Damage location | Amount of deformation | Kinks | Tears | Manufacturer restrictions | Some damaged structural components must be replaced. | Technicians should not assume that a component can be straightened simply because metal can physically be moved. | Why Do Modern Structural Materials Matter?
